title: Grandpa's Red Kite
sum: Rosie and Grandpa fix his old red kite and learn to read the wind, until Rosie flies it by herself on Kite Day.

cast.d: a six-year-old girl who finds Grandpa's old kite in the shed
cast.look: a six-year-old girl with curly brown hair, a yellow sweater and green rubber boots

cast.d: Rosie's grandpa, who made the red kite with his dad when he was seven
cast.look: a tall grandpa with white hair, a gray flat cap and a blue checked shirt

cast.d: Grandpa's small dog, who likes crackers and socks
cast.look: a small brown dog with floppy ears and a white nose

p: Creeeak! Grandpa's shed door swung open. Inside, it smelled like dust and old wood. Achoo! Rosie sneezed, and then Biscuit sneezed too.
Grandpa was looking for his rake. Rosie was looking at everything else. Behind a stack of flowerpots, something red poked out.
It was flat and wrapped in an old sheet. Rosie gave the sheet a tug, and it slid to the floor. Under it was a kite, as red as a fire truck.
“Grandpa, look!” Rosie stood it up on the floor. It came all the way up to her chin.
Grandpa turned around. His eyebrows went up, up, up. “My old red kite,” he said. “I made it with my dad when I was seven.”
The kite was a diamond, with four pointy corners. Its long string tail had little cloth bows tied along it.
Rosie counted the bows. “One, two, three, four, five, six.” They were gray and raggedy. In between were long, bare bits of string.
“It had ten bows once,” said Grandpa. “I think the mice nibbled the rest.” Biscuit sniffed the tail. He looked very interested in mice.
“Can it still fly?” Rosie asked. Grandpa scratched his chin. “Not with a bald tail. It needs all ten bows, or it will spin like a top.”
So Rosie got to work. First she pulled the pink ribbon out of her hair. She tied it on the tail. Seven.
Next, Grandpa found an old yellow dish towel with a hole in it. Rosie tore off a strip and tied that on. Eight.
Then Rosie grabbed a green sock off the shelf. “Hey, that's my sock!” said Grandpa. Rosie wiggled a finger through the hole in the toe. Grandpa sighed. “Fine.” Snip, snip. Nine.
The last bow came from a blue shirt in the rag box. Rosie pulled the knot tight. “Ten!”
Grandpa's yard ran up to the bottom of Windy Hill. Out on the grass, Grandpa pulled up a few blades. He held them high and let go.
The grass did not fall straight down. It floated sideways, toward the house. “The wind is coming down the hill,” said Grandpa. “Not too much. Not too little.”
Rosie tried it too. Her grass blew right into Biscuit's face. Achoo! Poor Biscuit.
Grandpa held the kite up, with its red face to the wind. Rosie gripped the spool with both hands. “Hold on tight,” he said.
A puff of wind came, and Grandpa let go. The kite shivered, then climbed. Up past the fence. Up past the apple tree.
“It's flying!” Rosie shouted. The string tugged at her fingers. All ten bows wiggled and waved.
It was only a small wind, so the kite did not go very high. But it stayed up. It did not spin once.
“When I was seven,” said Grandpa, “I flew it over Windy Hill. All by myself.” Rosie looked up at the big hill. “Me too,” she said. “One day.”
Biscuit barked up at the kite. Woof! That meant yes.

art.s: A girl with curly brown hair holds a string spool as an old red diamond kite with a tail of mixed-color cloth bows rises over a backyard apple tree, while her white-haired grandpa and a small brown dog look up.

q.q: Why did Grandpa hold up grass and let it go?
q.e: The grass floated toward the house. It showed which way the wind was blowing.

q.q: Draw Rosie when the kite went up. Add a speech bubble with what she shouted.
look: the red kite in the sky
q.e: What a happy picture! You can almost hear Rosie shout.

q.q: The tail had six old bows. How many new bows did Rosie tie on?
q.e: Pink, yellow, green and blue. Six and four more make ten!

p: On Saturday, Rosie and Grandpa climbed Windy Hill. Grandpa carried the red kite. Rosie carried the snack bag. Biscuit carried nothing and ran ahead.
The path was steep. Puff, puff went Rosie. At the top there was a wooden bench and a whole lot of sky.
But something was wrong. The grass stood still. The bushes stood still. Rosie dropped a few blades of grass to test the wind. They fell straight down onto her boot.
“No wind,” said Grandpa. “Not one puff.” Rosie did not want to wait. She grabbed the spool. Grandpa held up the kite, and she ran.
The kite bumped along the grass. Then it lifted and wobbled up behind her. She ran faster. It rose a little higher.
Then Rosie stopped to catch her breath. The kite stopped too. Flop! It landed on the grass like a pancake.
“Why did it go up when I ran?” Rosie asked. “Running makes a little wind,” said Grandpa. “The air pushes on the kite. But your legs get tired before the sky does.”
Rosie tried two more times. Flop. Flop. Her cheeks got hot and pink. At last she flopped down on the bench, just like the kite.
Grandpa opened the snack bag. He gave Rosie four crackers and kept four for himself. Rosie lined hers up on her knee.
A brown nose poked out from under the bench. Chomp! One of Rosie's crackers was gone. Biscuit licked his lips.
“Biscuit!” said Rosie. Biscuit wagged his tail. He did not look sorry at all. Rosie tried to frown, but a giggle came out instead.
“Now we wait,” said Grandpa. “The wind comes when it wants to.” He pointed down the hill at a farm. Mrs. Patel's white sheets hung on her clothesline.
“Watch those sheets,” said Grandpa. “When they flap, the wind is here.” The sheets hung straight down. They did not move one bit.
Grandpa began to sing his old kite song. “Wind, wind, come and play. Lift my kite up high today!” “Play, today!” said Rosie. “They rhyme!”
She sang it too, even louder. Biscuit put his nose in the air and howled along. Aroooo!
Down at the farm, one sheet gave a little wave. Then another. Soon all of them were flapping. Flap, flap, flap!
The grass began to shiver. Rosie's hair blew across her face. She dropped some grass, and it sailed off ahead of her.
“Now!” said Grandpa. He held the kite up high and let go. The wind caught it at once.
Up went the red kite, higher than the trees. Its long tail swished and swayed. Rosie did not have to run one step.
Down at the farm, Mrs. Patel's sheets waved and waved. They looked like they were cheering.

art.s: On a grassy hilltop with a wooden bench, a girl holds the string of a rising red diamond kite while her grandpa points down at white sheets flapping on a farm clothesline, and a small brown dog licks cracker crumbs.

q.q: Rosie had four crackers. Biscuit ate one. How many did she have left?
q.e: Four take away one is three. Biscuit had the other one!

q.q: How could Rosie tell the wind had come?
q.e: Flap, flap! The sheets, the grass and Rosie's hair all moved. That's how you spot the wind.

q.q: Draw Biscuit with Rosie's cracker. Add a speech bubble. What would Biscuit say?
look: a speech bubble for Biscuit, like “Yum!”
q.e: Ha! Biscuit did not look one bit sorry. Now your bubble lets him talk back.

p: A few days later, the wind came back, big and wild. The trees on Windy Hill went whoosh, whoosh. Rosie's scarf blew straight out, like a flag.
Rosie held the spool with both hands. Grandpa stood right behind her, just in case. The red kite zoomed up fast. All ten bows on its tail snapped and fluttered.
The kite tugged and tugged. Rosie leaned back and dug her boot heels into the grass. “It's so strong!” she said.
Then the wind swung around. The kite dipped and spun. It swooped down, right into the big oak tree. Crunch! Rustle!
“The tree ate our kite!” Rosie shouted. The kite hung upside down in the branches. Only its tail swung free.
Rosie gave the string a tug. The branches held on tight. “Stop,” said Grandpa. “If you pull hard, the paper will rip.”
They walked up to the oak. Rosie patted its trunk. It was wide and bumpy, like a crocodile's back. An acorn cap crunched under her boot.
Grandpa reached up with his walking stick. Too short. He stood on his tiptoes. Still too short.
“I'll find a longer one,” said Rosie. Three sticks lay under the tree. The first was shorter than her arm. The second was as long as a broom.
The third stick was the longest of all. It was almost as long as Grandpa! Rosie dragged it over. Bump, bump, bump.
Bonk! Something hit Grandpa's cap. Bonk! Another one. Two acorns rolled onto the grass, each one wearing a tiny hat.
Up on a branch sat a gray squirrel. It flicked its bushy tail. Biscuit barked. Woof! The squirrel did not care one bit.
Grandpa rubbed the top of his head. “He thinks this is his tree.” Rosie giggled.
Grandpa lifted Rosie up onto his shoulders. She held the long stick with both hands. Up, up, a little to the left. Poke. Wiggle. Poke.
Leaves pattered down onto Grandpa's cap. Then the kite slipped off the branch. Down it floated, like a big red leaf. Rosie slid down Grandpa's back and ran to it.
The kite was fine. Well, almost fine. One corner had a small rip. And the tail looked shorter than before.
Rosie looked back up at the oak. One of the old gray bows was still up there, caught on a twig. The squirrel ran out along the branch and sniffed it.
Then it grabbed the bow in its teeth. Zip! It dashed into a hole in the trunk. “Hey, that's ours!” said Rosie.
Grandpa laughed. “Well, now his nest has a blanket.” Rosie picked up an acorn and put it in her pocket. “You keep the bow,” she called up. “I'll keep this.”

art.s: A grandpa in a gray cap holds a girl on his shoulders as she pokes a long stick at a red diamond kite stuck upside down in a big oak tree, while a gray squirrel watches from a branch and acorns lie in the grass.

q.q: The tail had ten bows. The squirrel took one. How many were left?
q.e: Ten take away one is nine. One less bow!

q.q: What sound did the acorn make when it hit Grandpa's cap?
q.e: Bonk! Sound words make a story fun to read out loud.

q.q: Draw the oak tree with the kite stuck in it. Show the trunk, branches and leaves.
look: the red kite caught in the branches
q.e: What a tree! Trunk, branches and leaves are all parts of a tree.

p: Pitter, patter, pat. Rain tapped on Grandpa's kitchen window all morning. Rosie pressed her nose to the cold glass. She could not even see Windy Hill.
Tomorrow was Kite Day. The whole town would fly kites on the hill. “What if it still rains?” asked Rosie.
Fat gray clouds hung low over the roofs. “Those are rain clouds,” said Grandpa. “Thick and gray, and full of water.”
“Can't we fly the kite in the rain?” Rosie asked. Grandpa found a scrap of red paper, the same kind as the kite. He dripped water on it from a spoon. Drip, drip.
Rosie poked the wet spot. It was soft and floppy. She poked it again, and her finger went right through. “Oops!”
“Wet paper is weak,” said Grandpa. “And heavy. A wet kite would sag and tear.” So they fixed the kite inside instead.
First they mended the little rip from the oak tree. Rosie held the kite flat on the table. Grandpa cut a piece of clear tape. Rosie pressed it on and smoothed it with her thumb.
Then she turned the kite over. On the back, two thin sticks made a cross. One went from top to bottom. The other went from side to side.
“Look, Grandpa! Shapes!” The sticks cut the big diamond into smaller triangles. Rosie traced each one with her finger and counted.
Next came the tail. Rosie counted the bows. Nine. The squirrel had one in his nest now. “We need one more,” she said.
The rag box was out in the shed. The shed was out in the rain. They looked in the kitchen drawer instead. Only spoons and string.
Just then Biscuit trotted in. Something green hung from his mouth. It was a green sock, the twin of the one already on the tail.
“Not my other green sock!” said Grandpa. Biscuit wagged his tail. Grandpa looked at the soggy, chewed sock. Then he laughed. “Oh, fine. Now the socks can fly together.”
Rosie cut a strip and tied a floppy green bow. Ten again. Biscuit sniffed it, just to check.
Every kite at Kite Day got a name card. Rosie took a fat crayon and wrote three words about the kite. RED. OLD. BRAVE.
“Brave?” asked Grandpa. “It fought an oak tree,” said Rosie. “And it won.”
The rain kept tapping. Rosie went back to the window and sang. “Rain, rain, go away. We need wind for Kite Day!”
“You made your own rhyme,” said Grandpa. Then he sang it with her in his deep, rumbly voice. Biscuit thumped his tail. Thump, thump.
By suppertime, the tapping stopped. The gray clouds began to slide away over the hill. Behind them, the sky was pale and clean.
Then the treetops began to sway. Rosie pressed her nose to the glass again. “Grandpa,” she whispered. “Wind.”

art.s: On a rainy day in a cozy kitchen, a girl presses tape onto a red diamond kite on the table while her grandpa laughs and a small brown dog trots in with a green sock in its mouth.

q.q: Rosie sang, “Rain, rain, go away.” Which word did she rhyme with “away”?
q.e: Away, Day. They end with the same sound, so they rhyme!

q.q: What happened when Grandpa dripped water on the paper?
q.e: Wet paper goes soft and weak. That's why the kite stayed inside.

q.q: Draw the kite with its two crossed sticks. How many small triangles can you find?
q.e: Two crossed sticks cut the diamond into four small triangles. Super shape spotting!

p: Kite Day was bright and blowy. On the way up the hill, Rosie's hat blew off twice. The second time, Grandpa tucked it into his pocket.
Windy Hill was full of people. Kites dipped and swooped everywhere. There was a green fish and a blue bird. There was a long orange dragon with a curly tail.
Rosie counted every kite in the sky. One, two, three, four, five, six, seven. Seven kites, and not one of them was red.
At the top, Grandpa stopped. He gave Rosie the kite and the spool. Then he put his hands in his pockets. “Today you fly it,” he said. “All by yourself.”
Rosie's tummy went wobbly. What if the kite crashed? What if it hit a tree? She peeked down at the big oak. It looked hungry.
Rosie held the kite up high and let go. But it did not climb. It flipped over and flopped down, right at her feet.
“Hmm,” said Grandpa. “What do we do first?” Rosie thought hard. Then she remembered.
She pulled up a few blades of grass and let them go. They blew back past her ears. The wind was in her face! She was standing the wrong way.
Rosie turned all the way around. Now the wind pushed on her back. She held the kite up again and waited for a big puff.
Here it came. Whoosh! Rosie let go, and the wind slid under the red kite. Up it went. She let out the string, a little at a time.
The kite climbed past the fish. It climbed past the bird. It climbed until it was higher than the orange dragon.
The string pulled at Rosie's hands, but she held on. Every bow on the tail danced. The old gray ones danced. So did the pink, the yellow and the blue.
The two green sock bows danced most of all. Rosie laughed. Grandpa's socks had never been so high.
Rosie counted the kites in the sky again. This time, one of them was hers.
Grandpa sat down on the bench with Biscuit. He watched the red kite for a long time. “When I was seven,” he said, “I flew it just like that. All by myself.”
Biscuit spotted the kite's shadow sliding over the grass. He chased it. He pounced on it. The shadow slid away, and off he went again.
A boy with the dragon kite came over. “Whose kite is that?” he asked. Rosie looked at Grandpa. Grandpa looked at Rosie. “Ours,” they said together.
Then Rosie sang Grandpa's old song. “Wind, wind, come and play. Lift my kite up high today!” High above Windy Hill, the red kite wiggled its bows, like it was waving.

art.s: On a sunny, windy hill full of kites, including a green fish, a blue bird and a long orange dragon, a girl flies a red diamond kite with a long bowed tail while her grandpa sits on a bench with a small brown dog.

q.q: After the kite flopped, what did Rosie do first?
q.e: First she dropped grass to find the wind. Next she turned around. Then up went the kite!

q.q: Seven kites were flying. Then the red kite went up. How many kites were flying then?
q.e: Seven and one more makes eight!

q.q: Draw the wind lifting the red kite. Use arrows to show where the wind pushes.
look: the red kite high in the sky
arrows pushing up under the kite
Rosie with the wind at her back
q.e: You drew the wind! We can't see wind, but arrows can show it.

fin.q: How many bows were on the kite's tail on Kite Day?
fin.e: Six old bows and four new ones made ten. The squirrel took one, and the sock bow made ten again.

fin.q: Which kind of day was best for flying the red kite?
fin.e: A kite needs wind to lift it. On the still day it flopped, and rain makes paper soft.
